notions.question: How do British institutions work without a single written constitution?
notions.definition: The United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary system. Its constitution is not codified in a single text: it rests on Acts of Parliament (statutes), court decisions, constitutional conventions and historical documents. The Westminster Parliament comprises the monarch, the House of Commons, elected by universal suffrage (650 seats), and the House of Lords, which is unelected (appointed life peers, a limited number of hereditary peers, bishops of the Church of England). Under the principle of parliamentary sovereignty, Parliament can pass or repeal any law. The Prime Minister is the leader of the party that holds a majority in the Commons; he or she forms the government and the Cabinet, which are collectively responsible to the Commons. The monarch reigns but does not rule.

lignes: Head of State; symbolic and ceremonial role (Royal Assent to bills, King's/Queen's Speech)
650 elected Members of Parliament (MPs); passes laws and the budget; scrutinises the government
Unelected chamber; examines and amends bills; power of delay limited by the Parliament Acts (1911, 1949)
Government drawn from the majority in the Commons, collective responsibility
Second-largest party in the Commons, "shadow cabinet"

termes.definition: A monarchy whose powers are limited by the constitution.
The elected lower house.
The supremacy of Acts of Parliament.
The Opposition team that mirrors the ministers.

exemple.texte: In a commentary, one would point out that a British Prime Minister can change in the middle of a Parliament without a general election, when his or her party changes leader: it is the majority in the Commons, not a direct popular vote, that underpins the Prime Minister's power.

confusions.explication: The United Kingdom does have a constitution, but it is spread across statutes, conventions and case law.

verification: What is the British Prime Minister's power based on?
notions.aVerifier: Composition of the House of Lords (reform of hereditary peers launched in 2024-2025): check on parliament.uk.

notions.question: Why do two parties dominate British political life?
notions.definition: General elections to the House of Commons use the single-member plurality system (first past the post): in each of the 650 constituencies, the candidate who comes first is elected, even without an absolute majority. This system favours the two main parties, the Conservative Party ("Tories") and the Labour Party, and disadvantages parties whose votes are spread thinly (Liberal Democrats, Reform UK, Greens), while allowing regionally concentrated parties (Scottish National Party) to win many seats. It often produces clear majorities on a minority of the vote. A 2011 referendum rejected a switch to the Alternative Vote. The July 2024 general election returned Labour to power with a large majority.

lignes: Moderate left; public services, historically the trade unions

termes.es: sistema mayoritario uninominal a una vuelta
termes.definition: The candidate who comes first is elected.
An area that elects one MP.
Domination by two parties.

exemple.texte: With 35% of the vote spread evenly, one party can win more than half the seats; with 15% spread thinly, another may win only a handful: this is the amplifying effect of the plurality system.

confusions.explication: Historical terms; "Tory" is still commonly used to mean a Conservative.

verification: Why does first past the post favour a two-party system?

flashcards.reponse: Constitutional monarchy, parliamentary system, uncodified constitution (statutes, conventions, case law), parliamentary sovereignty. Prime Minister = leader of the majority party in the Commons; Cabinet collectively responsible; Opposition and shadow cabinet. First past the post → two-party system Conservatives / Labour, clear majorities, thinly spread parties disadvantaged, SNP favoured by its concentration.

notions.question: Why is an official report from 1942 regarded as the founding act of the British Welfare State?
notions.definition: Published in early December 1942, in the middle of the war, the report "Social Insurance and Allied Services" by the Liberal economist William Beveridge proposed a universal social security system to fight the "five giants": Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness (that is, unemployment). It provided for a single national social insurance scheme financed by flat-rate contributions, giving entitlement to flat-rate benefits "from the cradle to the grave", and it assumed a national health service, family allowances and a policy of full employment. Hugely popular, it gave post-war reconstruction a programme.

termes.definition: A state that guarantees extensive social protection.
A protection scheme financed by contributions.
Benefits for everyone, without means-testing.

exemple.texte: The report, published in December 1942 under the title Social Insurance and Allied Services (Cmd. 6404), sold hundreds of thousands of copies and identified the "five giants" to be defeated.

confusions.explication: The report was the work of a Liberal under a coalition government; its implementation fell to Labour.

verification: Name the five "giants" of the Beveridge Report.

notions.titre: Attlee and the Welfare State: the NHS
notions.question: How did Labour build the Welfare State after 1945?
notions.definition: In July 1945, against all expectations, Clement Attlee's Labour Party heavily defeated Churchill's Conservatives. The Attlee government (1945-1951) implemented Beveridge's recommendations: the National Insurance Act (1946) and family allowances, the National Assistance Act (1948), and above all the National Health Service, created by the National Health Service Act 1946 and launched on 5 July 1948 under the leadership of the Minister of Health Aneurin Bevan: care free at the point of use, financed by taxation, for the whole population. To this were added nationalisations and a housebuilding policy. The Education Act 1944 (Butler), passed under the coalition, had already made free secondary education universal.

lignes: National Insurance Act; National Health Service Act

termes.definition: The British public health system, free at the point of use.

termes.en: free at the point of use
termes.es: gratuito en el punto de uso
termes.definition: No direct payment by the patient.
A large election victory.

exemple.texte: The NHS was launched on 5 July 1948, following the National Health Service Act 1946 steered through by Aneurin Bevan.

verification: Who was behind the NHS and when was it launched?

notions.question: Which sectors did the British state take over after 1945, and why?
notions.definition: In line with Clause IV of the Labour Party constitution (common ownership of the means of production), the Attlee government nationalised the sectors regarded as strategic or failing: the Bank of England (1946), civil aviation (1946), coal (1947, National Coal Board), inland transport including the railways (1948), electricity (1948), gas (1949), then iron and steel (1951, denationalised by the Conservatives in 1953 and renationalised in 1967). Around a fifth of the economy came under public control. Aims: to modernise ageing industries, guarantee employment and plan reconstruction. These public corporations would be at the heart of debates on efficiency and decline, before the privatisations of the 1980s.

lignes: Iron and steel (denationalised in 1953, renationalised in 1967)

termes.definition: The transfer of a company to the public sector.
The coexistence of public and private sectors.
The article of the Labour constitution on common ownership, rewritten in 1995.

exemple.texte: A commentary on a 1947 poster proclaiming "Today the mines belong to the people" can be linked to the nationalisation of coal and to Clause IV.

confusions.explication: After privatisation, the state regulates rather than owns.

verification: Why does iron and steel illustrate the alternation of power in British politics?

flashcards.question: Tell the story of the birth of the British Welfare State, from Beveridge to Attlee.
flashcards.reponse: 1942: Beveridge Report (Social Insurance and Allied Services) against the five giants (Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness), universal protection "from the cradle to the grave". 1944: Education Act (Butler). July 1945: Labour victory under Attlee. 1946: National Insurance Act, NHS Act; 5 July 1948: launch of the NHS (Bevan), free and financed by taxation. Nationalisations: Bank of England (1946), coal (1947), rail and electricity (1948), gas (1949), steel (1951); a mixed economy in the name of Clause IV.
erreurs: Attributing the NHS to Beveridge or to Churchill

notions.question: Why do we speak of a "consensus" between Conservatives and Labour from 1945 to the 1970s?
notions.definition: Back in power in 1951, the Conservatives (Churchill, Eden, Macmillan) kept most of the Labour legacy. Despite their differences, the two main parties then shared common ground: preservation of the Welfare State and the NHS, a mixed economy, the goal of full employment through Keynesian demand management, and a recognised role for the trade unions in negotiations (corporatism). The term "Butskellism", coined in 1954 by the weekly The Economist, merges the names of Rab Butler (Conservative Chancellor of the Exchequer) and Hugh Gaitskell (his Labour predecessor), to stress the continuity of their economic policies. The existence and extent of this consensus are debated by historians.

items: Mixed economy: the nationalisations are largely kept (except steel and road haulage)
Gradual decolonisation and the special relationship with the United States

termes.definition: Tacit agreement between the main parties on economic and social fundamentals.
A policy of supporting demand to achieve full employment.
The British finance minister.

exemple.texte: In a 1957 speech, a Conservative Prime Minister claiming that the British have "never had it so good" illustrates the confidence of the consensus era in growth and full employment.

confusions.explication: Thatcherism defined itself precisely against this consensus.

verification: Where does the term "Butskellism" come from?

notions.question: Why is the United Kingdom described as a country in decline in the 1960s and 1970s?
notions.definition: Despite real growth, the United Kingdom experienced relative decline after 1945: its growth and productivity were lower than those of West Germany, France or Japan, its share of world trade shrank and the Empire was dismantled. Economic policy alternated between phases of expansion (go) and restraint (stop): expansion led to inflation and a balance-of-payments deficit, which weakened sterling and forced a slowdown (higher interest rates, credit restrictions). The pound was devalued in 1949 and again in 1967 (Wilson government). Causes put forward: underinvestment, confrontational industrial relations, technological lag, the burden of military spending and of sterling's role as a reserve currency. The expression "sick man of Europe" took hold in the 1970s.

etapes: Go: demand is boosted (tax cuts, credit)
Slowdown, unemployment, then a new expansion

termes.definition: Falling behind other countries, despite absolute growth.
An official reduction in the value of a currency.
The account of transactions with the rest of the world.

exemple.texte: A graph comparing British, German and French growth rates from 1950 to 1973 can illustrate relative decline: the United Kingdom progresses, but more slowly.

confusions.explication: British living standards rise, but more slowly than those of its neighbours.

notions.question: Why did the United Kingdom join the European Community so late?
notions.definition: The United Kingdom declined to take part in the ECSC (1951) and the EEC (1957), giving priority to the Commonwealth, the special relationship with the United States and its sovereignty; in 1960 it founded the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). Seeing the dynamism of the EEC, it applied in 1961 (Macmillan) and again in 1967 (Wilson), and was rejected both times by General de Gaulle's veto (1963 and 1967). It finally joined on 1 January 1973, under Edward Heath's Conservative government, together with Ireland and Denmark. Labour, divided, held a referendum in June 1975 on remaining in the Community: "Yes" won with about 67% of the vote. The relationship would remain ambivalent (rebate secured by Thatcher in 1984, Maastricht opt-outs, the 2016 referendum and withdrawal in 2020).

termes.definition: Joining an organisation.
Hostile to or wary of European integration.
The privileged link between the United Kingdom and the United States.

exemple.texte: A leaflet from the 1975 campaign urging a "Yes" vote in the name of jobs and peace can be compared with the 2016 arguments to gauge how the European debate has changed.

verification: Why did the 1961 and 1967 applications fail?

notions.titre: The crisis of the 1970s and the Winter of Discontent
notions.question: How did the crisis of the 1970s pave the way for Margaret Thatcher?
notions.definition: The 1970s saw the end of the consensus. The Heath government (1970-1974) faced the miners' strikes (1972, 1974) and the first oil shock (1973), and imposed the three-day week (early 1974) to save energy; it lost the February 1974 election after asking the question "Who governs Britain?". Labour (Wilson, then Callaghan) faced stagflation (inflation above 20% in 1975, rising unemployment) and in 1976 had to seek an IMF loan, which came with spending cuts. Its incomes policy collapsed during the winter of 1978-1979, the "Winter of Discontent": mass strikes in the public sector (refuse collectors, transport, hospitals). The Callaghan government fell on a vote of no confidence in March 1979; Margaret Thatcher's Conservatives won the May 1979 general election.

termes.definition: Inflation combined with stagnation and unemployment.
The wave of strikes of the winter of 1978-1979.
A vote that brings down the government.

exemple.texte: A 1978 Conservative poster showing a queue outside an employment office, with the slogan "Labour isn't working", can be analysed as a document from the campaign that brought Thatcher to power.

verification: Why did the winter of 1978-1979 discredit Labour?

flashcards.question: Trace Britain's development from 1951 to 1979: consensus, decline, Europe, crisis.
flashcards.reponse: Consensus (Butskellism, 1954: Butler + Gaitskell): Welfare State, mixed economy, Keynesianism, full employment, consultation with the unions. Relative decline: weaker growth than its neighbours, stop-go, devaluations of 1949 and 1967, "sick man of Europe". Europe: EEC turned down (1957), EFTA (1960), de Gaulle's vetoes (1963, 1967), accession on 1 January 1973 (Heath), 1975 referendum (≈ 67% Yes). Crisis: miners' strikes, oil shock, three-day week (1974), IMF (1976), Winter of Discontent (1978-1979), Thatcher's victory (May 1979).

notions.question: What economic policy did Margaret Thatcher set against the Keynesian consensus?
notions.definition: Inspired by the economists Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, Margaret Thatcher (Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990) made the fight against inflation her priority, at the expense of full employment. Monetarism means controlling the growth of the money supply (Medium-Term Financial Strategy, 1980), reducing the budget deficit and keeping interest rates high. The policy went hand in hand with "rolling back the frontiers of the state": cuts in income tax, deregulation, privatisation, curbs on trade union power. In the short term, the 1980-1981 recession pushed unemployment above three million and hit Northern industry hard; inflation fell markedly in the mid-1980s. Strict monetarism was gradually relaxed.

items: Priority: price stability, control of the money supply
Cuts in public spending and in the deficit
"There is no alternative" (TINA): refusal to return to reflationary policies

termes.definition: A doctrine giving priority to controlling the money supply in order to fight inflation.
The amount of money in circulation.
The decline of industry within the economy.

exemple.texte: The phrase "The lady's not for turning" (1980 Conservative Party conference) can be discussed as a refusal to make an economic U-turn despite rising unemployment.

confusions.explication: The former targets inflation through money; the latter targets full employment through demand.

verification: What were the immediate social consequences of monetarism?

notions.question: Why and how did Thatcher privatise the major public corporations?
notions.definition: The Thatcher governments sold most of the nationalised industries to the private sector: British Telecom (1984), British Gas (1986, with the "Tell Sid" advertising campaign), British Airways and Rolls-Royce (1987), British Steel (1988), the water companies (1989), electricity (1990-1991). Aims: efficiency through competition and profit, revenue for the state, reduced trade union influence, and the creation of a "popular capitalism" through individual share ownership. The right of council tenants to buy their homes (Right to Buy, Housing Act 1980) followed the same logic of a "property-owning democracy". The record is debated: efficiency gains in some sectors, but concentration of share ownership, price rises and private monopolies requiring regulators.

termes.definition: The sale of a public corporation to the private sector.
The spread of share ownership across the population.
The option for tenants to buy their home.

exemple.texte: An "If you see Sid, tell him" advertisement (British Gas, 1986) can be analysed as a tool for promoting popular share ownership.

confusions.explication: Privatisation changes the owner; deregulation loosens the rules.

verification: What were the political aims of privatisation?

notions.titre: The trade unions and the miners' strike
notions.question: How did Thatcher reduce the power of the trade unions?
notions.definition: Seeing union power as a cause of decline and of the crises of the 1970s, the Thatcher governments curbed it through successive laws: the Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 (limits on picketing, secondary action and the closed shop) and the Trade Union Act 1984 (compulsory secret ballot before a strike). The decisive conflict was the miners' strike (March 1984 - March 1985), led by Arthur Scargill's National Union of Mineworkers against the closure of pits deemed uneconomic by the National Coal Board. Called without a national ballot and marked by violent clashes (Orgreave, June 1984), it ended in defeat for the miners. Union membership and the number of strike days then fell lastingly.

lignes: Employment Acts: picketing, secondary action, closed shop
Trade Union Act: secret ballot before a strike

termes.definition: An organisation that defends employees.
A group of strikers outside the workplace.
The requirement to be a union member in order to be hired.

exemple.texte: A photograph of miners facing mounted police in 1984 can be discussed as a symbol of the confrontation between the government and working-class trade unionism.

verification: Why is the 1984-1985 miners' strike a turning point?

notions.titre: The Big Bang in the City (1986)
notions.question: How did the City of London become a leading global financial centre?
notions.definition: The "Big Bang" refers to the sudden deregulation of the London Stock Exchange on 27 October 1986: abolition of fixed commissions, end of the separation between brokers and market makers (jobbers), opening of stockbroking firms' capital to banks, including foreign ones, and the switch to electronic trading. Prepared by the abolition of exchange controls (1979), the reform attracted the major international banks and made the City one of the world's leading financial centres. It contributed to the growth of financial services, but also to the financialisation of the economy, to regional inequalities and to risk-taking that was criticised after the 2008 crisis.

items: 27 October 1986: Big Bang (negotiable commissions, end of the broker / jobber separation, foreign banks admitted, electronic trading)
Consequences: boom in the City, takeovers of British firms by foreign banks, "yuppie" culture
Debates: weight of finance, gap between London and the former industrial regions

termes.definition: Removing or loosening the rules governing a sector.
A city where financial activities are concentrated.
Restrictions on currency movements.

exemple.texte: A 1986 press article describing trading floors deserted in favour of screens illustrates the switch to electronic trading.

confusions.explication: Two different strands of Thatcherite liberalisation.

verification: Which measures made up the 1986 Big Bang?

notions.titre: The poll tax and Thatcher's downfall
notions.question: Why did Margaret Thatcher leave office in 1990?
notions.definition: The "poll tax" (officially the Community Charge) replaced local taxes based on the value of homes with a flat-rate charge per adult, regardless of income. Introduced in Scotland in 1989 and then in England and Wales in April 1990, it was seen as deeply unfair and provoked widespread non-payment and violent demonstrations (London, 31 March 1990). Divisions over Europe added to this: the resignation of Deputy Prime Minister Geoffrey Howe and his resignation speech (November 1990) triggered Michael Heseltine's challenge for the party leadership. With insufficient support in the first round, Thatcher withdrew and resigned at the end of November 1990; John Major succeeded her. The poll tax was replaced by the council tax (1993).

lignes: Poll tax in England and Wales
Geoffrey Howe's resignation and speech; Heseltine's challenge; Thatcher withdraws

termes.definition: A flat-rate tax per person.
A tax that funds local authorities.
Voluntarily leaving a post.

exemple.texte: A 1990 cartoon showing Thatcher surrounded by ministers brandishing knives can be discussed in connection with the Conservative Party revolt.

confusions.explication: Thatcher did not lose a general election: she was removed by her own party.

flashcards.question: Outline Thatcherism: economic policy, privatisation, trade unions, the City, downfall.
flashcards.reponse: Monetarism (Friedman, Hayek): priority to inflation, money supply, high interest rates, spending cuts; 1980-1981 recession, more than 3 million unemployed; TINA. Privatisation: BT (1984), British Gas (1986), BA (1987), water (1989), electricity (1990-1991); Right to Buy (1980); popular capitalism. Trade unions: Employment Acts 1980, 1982, Trade Union Act 1984; miners' strike 1984-1985 (Scargill) lost. Big Bang (27 October 1986): deregulation of the City. Downfall: poll tax (1989-1990), divisions over Europe, Howe's resignation, Heseltine's challenge, departure in November 1990; succeeded by Major.
erreurs: Saying that Thatcher lost an election

notions.question: How did John Major govern after Thatcher, and why did he lose in 1997?
notions.definition: John Major succeeded Thatcher in November 1990. He replaced the poll tax with the council tax, took part in the Gulf War (1991) and narrowly won the 1992 general election. On 16 September 1992 ("Black Wednesday"), sterling, under speculative attack, had to leave the European Exchange Rate Mechanism: the Conservatives' economic credibility collapsed, even though growth later returned. The party tore itself apart over the Maastricht Treaty (ratified in 1993, with opt-outs for the United Kingdom on the single currency and the Social Chapter), and the government was weakened by scandals ("sleaze"). Major continued privatisation (coal, railways) and launched the peace process in Northern Ireland (Downing Street Declaration, 1993). Tony Blair's Labour Party won by a wide margin on 1 May 1997.

lignes: Black Wednesday: exit from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism
Ratification of Maastricht; Downing Street Declaration; council tax

termes.definition: 16 September 1992: sterling forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
Exemption from taking part in a European policy.
Scandals involving politicians.

exemple.texte: A graph of the pound's exchange rate in September 1992 can be used to discuss Black Wednesday and the Conservatives' loss of economic credibility.

confusions.a: Exit from the Exchange Rate Mechanism (1992)

verification: Why did Black Wednesday weaken the Conservatives?

notions.titre: New Labour and the Third Way
notions.question: In what ways did Tony Blair's New Labour break with traditional Labourism?
notions.definition: After becoming Labour leader in 1994, Tony Blair modernised the party: Clause IV was rewritten in 1995 (dropping the goal of common ownership of the means of production), a "New Labour" image was adopted and the party distanced itself from the trade unions. The "Third Way", theorised in particular by the sociologist Anthony Giddens, seeks to move beyond the opposition between state socialism and neoliberalism: accepting the market economy and the Thatcherite legacy (no renationalisation), while investing in education, health and getting people into work (welfare to work). After the 1997 victory, the government gave the Bank of England independence over monetary policy (1997), created a national minimum wage (1998), passed the Human Rights Act (1998) and launched devolution. The record is tarnished by the Iraq War (2003). Gordon Brown succeeded Blair in 2007.

lignes: National Minimum Wage Act; Human Rights Act; Good Friday Agreement

termes.definition: A synthesis of market economics and social justice.
The legal minimum hourly pay.
A policy encouraging a return to work.

exemple.texte: The slogan "Tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime" can be discussed as an example of the New Labour synthesis of firmness and social action.

confusions.explication: Blair explicitly claimed to break with the old doctrine.

verification: Name three flagship reforms of the Blair government in 1997-1998.

notions.question: How did the United Kingdom transfer powers to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?
notions.definition: Devolution is the transfer of powers from the Westminster Parliament to elected institutions in the constituent nations, without federalism: Westminster remains sovereign. After the referendums of September 1997 (a large "Yes" in Scotland, a narrow "Yes" in Wales), the Scotland Act 1998 created the Scottish Parliament (Holyrood) with wide legislative powers (health, education, justice) and tax-raising powers; the Government of Wales Act 1998 created a Welsh Assembly, initially with limited powers, since extended (Senedd). The Northern Ireland Act 1998 set up a power-sharing Assembly arising from the Good Friday Agreement. Devolution raises the "West Lothian question" (Scottish MPs vote at Westminster on laws that concern only England) and has not extinguished Scottish nationalism (2014 independence referendum: 55% "No").

termes.definition: The transfer of powers to regional institutions.
Non-English MPs voting on English matters.
A vote on secession.

exemple.texte: Free university tuition for Scottish students in Scotland, unlike the English system, illustrates the Scottish Parliament's capacity to pursue its own policies.

confusions.explication: The United Kingdom remains a unitary state.

notions.question: How did the Good Friday Agreement bring the "Troubles" in Northern Ireland to an end?
notions.definition: The Northern Ireland conflict ("the Troubles", late 1960s - 1998) mainly pitted republicans / nationalists, mostly Catholic and in favour of unification with Ireland, against unionists / loyalists, mostly Protestant and attached to the United Kingdom; it claimed more than 3,500 lives. The Good Friday Agreement (or Belfast Agreement), signed on 10 April 1998 by the British and Irish governments and most of the Northern Ireland parties, was approved by referendum in the North and in the Republic of Ireland on 22 May 1998. It provides for: the principle of consent (Northern Ireland remains British for as long as a majority wishes), a power-sharing Assembly and Executive between the communities, North-South and East-West cooperation bodies, the amendment of Articles 2 and 3 of the Irish Constitution, the disarmament of paramilitary groups and the early release of prisoners. The question of the Irish border was at the heart of the Brexit negotiations.

items: Principle of consent of the majority of the population
Approved by twin referendums on 22 May 1998

termes.definition: A government bringing together both communities.
In favour of remaining in the United Kingdom.
In favour of a united Ireland.
Putting the weapons of armed groups beyond use.

exemple.texte: The Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998 and approved by referendum in Northern Ireland and in the Republic of Ireland on 22 May 1998.

confusions.explication: Hence the border issue after Brexit.

flashcards.reponse: Major (1990-1997): council tax, 1992 victory, Black Wednesday (16 September 1992), divisions over Maastricht, sleaze, rail privatisation, Downing Street Declaration (1993). notions.question: How should a historical or political document (speech, article, poster) be analysed in British civilisation?
notions.definition: The civilisation document commentary (often written in English) consists in presenting, explaining and interpreting a document by placing it in its historical context, without paraphrasing it. It comprises: an introduction presenting the document (nature, author, date, source, intended audience, context), its central question and its outline; a thematic (not line-by-line) development that explains the document's ideas by drawing on precise knowledge (dates, laws, actors) and quoting the text briefly; an analysis of the document's significance and limits (the author's point of view, intentions, what he or she leaves out); a conclusion that answers the central question and opens onto later historical developments.

etapes: Identify: nature (speech, editorial, poster, cartoon, statistics), author, date, source, audience
Contextualise: the political, economic and social situation at the time of the document
Bring out the main ideas and the devices used (rhetoric, images, figures)
Formulate a central question about the document's historical interest
Build a thematic outline in two or three parts
Write: short quotations, precise knowledge, critical perspective, conclusion with an opening

lignes: This document is an extract from a speech delivered by… on…
At the time, Britain was facing…
However, the author fails to mention… / This view should be qualified…
This document thus sheds light on… In the following years, …

termes.definition: A critical, contextualised analysis of a document.
Repeating the text in other words, to be avoided.
The historical importance of the document.

exemple.texte: Document: extract from a speech by Margaret Thatcher at the 1980 Conservative Party conference. Central question: how does this speech assert Thatcherism's break with the post-war consensus? I. An openly assumed economic break (monetarism, refusal of a "U-turn"); II. A political and moral vision (individual responsibility, the role of the state); III. A fighting speech in a context of recession (unemployment, protest).

confusions.explication: The examiner expects outside knowledge and a critical perspective.

verification: What should the presentation of a document include?

questions.enonce: Which practices are expected in a civilisation document commentary?

choix.texte: Placing the document in its historical context
Paraphrasing the text line by line
Analysing the author's point of view and intentions
Drawing on precise knowledge (dates, laws, actors)
choix.explication: It sheds light on the document.

choix.texte: A thematic outline answering a central question
A linear outline following the order of the paragraphs

flashcards.question: Describe the method of the civilisation document commentary.
flashcards.reponse: Identify (nature, author, date, source, audience); contextualise; bring out ideas and devices; central question on the document's historical interest; thematic outline in two or three parts; writing with short quotations, precise knowledge, analysis of the point of view and of omissions; conclusion answering the central question and opening onto what came next. Avoid paraphrase and a linear outline.

exercices.titre: Preparing a commentary on a 1945 Labour leaflet
exercices.enonce: Document (fictional, inspired by the manifestos of the time): a Labour leaflet from June 1945 promising "jobs for all", "a national health service" and "homes for the people", and recalling that "the Beveridge Report must be carried out in full".

questions.consigne: Write the introduction to the commentary (presentation, context, central question, outline).

criteres: Nature, issuer, date, intended audience (1945 voters)
Context: end of the war in Europe, July 1945 general election, Beveridge Report (1942)
Central question on post-war expectations and the Labour project
Outline announced in two or three parts
reponse.corrige: This document is an electoral leaflet issued by the Labour Party in June 1945, a few weeks before the general election of July 1945 and shortly after the end of the war in Europe. Addressed to voters who had endured six years of war, it promises full employment, a national health service and new housing, explicitly referring to the Beveridge Report of 1942, which had identified five "giants" to be defeated. How does this leaflet reflect the hopes of post-war Britain and announce the foundations of the Welfare State? We will first examine the social expectations it expresses, then the programme it puts forward, and finally its significance in the light of the Attlee governments' achievements (1945-1951).

correction: See the model answer and the criteria

synthese.titre: British civilisation: the UK since 1945 in 3 pages
synthese.essentiel: One storyline: Beveridge (1942) and Attlee (1945-1951) build the Welfare State and a mixed economy; both parties keep it (consensus, Butskellism) despite relative decline; the 1970s crisis ends the consensus; Thatcher (1979-1990) breaks with it (monetarism, privatisation, unions); Major and New Labour accept the market legacy and add social investment, devolution and peace in Northern Ireland.

chapitres.idee: A constitutional monarchy with an uncodified constitution, where Parliament is sovereign and the PM's power rests on a majority in the Commons won through first past the post.
points: Uncodified constitution: statutes, case law, conventions, historical documents (not 'no constitution')
Parliament = monarch + House of Commons (650 elected MPs) + House of Lords (unelected, delay limited by Parliament Acts 1911, 1949)
Parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can pass or repeal any law
PM = leader of the majority party in the Commons; Cabinet collectively responsible; Opposition has a shadow cabinet
The monarch reigns but does not rule (Royal Assent, King's Speech)
FPTP in 650 constituencies: favours Conservatives and Labour, clear majorities on a minority of votes, punishes spread-out parties, helps the concentrated SNP

dates.fait: Labour back in power with a large majority

distinctions.difference: The UK has a constitution, spread across statutes, conventions and case law.

questions.q: Can a British PM change without a general election? Why?
questions.r: Yes: power rests on the majority in the Commons; if the party changes leader, the PM changes.

questions.q: What are the effects of first past the post?
questions.r: Two-party system, clear majorities on a minority of votes, spread-out parties (Lib Dems, Greens, Reform UK) under-represented, concentrated SNP favoured.

questions.q: Who sits in the House of Lords?
questions.r: Unelected members: appointed life peers, a limited number of hereditary peers, Church of England bishops.

chapitres.idee: The Liberal Beveridge Report (1942) gave the programme; Attlee's Labour government (1945-1951) built it: social insurance, a free tax-funded NHS and nationalisations.
points: Beveridge Report, Dec 1942 (Social Insurance and Allied Services): universal cover 'from the cradle to the grave'
Five giants: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness (= unemployment)
Flat-rate contributions for flat-rate benefits; assumes an NHS, family allowances, full employment
July 1945: Attlee's landslide over Churchill; 1946 National Insurance Act; 1948 National Assistance Act
NHS (Act 1946, launched 5 July 1948, Aneurin Bevan): free at the point of use, financed by taxation
Nationalisations in the name of Clause IV: about a fifth of the economy under public control (mixed economy)

dates.fait: Bank of England, aviation (1946); coal (1947); rail, electricity (1948); gas (1949); steel (1951)

distinctions.difference: Report written under the wartime coalition; Labour put it into practice.
Financed by taxation versus financed by contributions.

chapitres.memo: Five giants, five answers: Want-insurance, Disease-NHS, Ignorance-education, Squalor-housing, Idleness-full employment.

questions.q: Name Beveridge's five giants.
questions.r: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness.

questions.q: When and by whom was the NHS launched, and how is it financed?
questions.r: 5 July 1948, Aneurin Bevan (Attlee government); free at the point of use, financed by taxation.

questions.q: Why did Attlee nationalise?
questions.r: Clause IV (common ownership); modernise ageing industries, guarantee jobs, plan reconstruction.

chapitres.idee: 1951-1979: both parties share the Welfare State and Keynesianism (consensus) amid relative decline, until the 1970s crisis breaks the model.
points: Consensus: Welfare State and NHS, mixed economy, Keynesian full employment, consultation with unions
'Butskellism' (The Economist, 1954) = Butler (Con) + Gaitskell (Lab): continuity of economic policy
Relative decline: growth slower than West Germany, France, Japan; 'sick man of Europe' (1970s)
Stop-go: expansion -> inflation, external deficit -> pressure on sterling -> restraint -> unemployment -> expansion
Europe: ECSC/EEC turned down, EFTA (1960), de Gaulle's vetoes, accession 1973 (Heath), 1975 referendum about 67% Yes
1970s: miners' strikes, oil shock, three-day week, stagflation, IMF loan, Winter of Discontent

dates.fait: Winter of Discontent; no confidence vote March 1979; Thatcher wins May 1979

distinctions.difference: Living standards rise, but more slowly than neighbours'.

questions.q: What does Butskellism mean?
questions.r: Term from The Economist (1954): Butler + Gaitskell, the continuity of Conservative and Labour economic policy in the consensus.

questions.q: Explain the stop-go cycle.
questions.r: Boosting demand -> imports, inflation, deficit -> sterling under pressure -> restraint (interest rates, credit) -> slowdown -> new expansion.

questions.q: Why did the UK join Europe late?
questions.r: Priority to Commonwealth, US special relationship, sovereignty; applications in 1961 and 1967 vetoed by de Gaulle; entry 1973.

questions.q: What was the Winter of Discontent?
questions.r: 1978-1979: collapse of Labour's incomes policy, mass public sector strikes; Callaghan falls (March 1979), Thatcher wins (May 1979).

chapitres.idee: Thatcher (1979-1990) broke with the consensus: inflation before full employment, rolling back the state, privatisation, curbing the unions and deregulating the City.
points: Monetarism (Friedman, Hayek): control money supply (MTFS 1980), cut deficit, high interest rates; TINA, 'The lady's not for turning'
Cost: 1980-1981 recession, over 3 million unemployed, deindustrialised North; inflation falls by mid-1980s
Privatisation: efficiency, state revenue, weaker unions, 'popular capitalism'; Right to Buy (1980) = 'property-owning democracy'
Unions: Employment Acts 1980, 1982 (picketing, secondary action, closed shop); Trade Union Act 1984 (secret ballot)
Miners' strike March 1984 - March 1985 (NUM, Scargill), no national ballot, Orgreave: miners defeated
Big Bang 27 Oct 1986: fixed commissions abolished, broker/jobber split ended, foreign banks, electronic trading
Downfall: poll tax (flat rate per adult), Europe divisions, Howe resigns, Heseltine challenge, she quits Nov 1990

dates.fait: BT / British Gas ('Tell Sid') / BA and Rolls-Royce

distinctions.difference: Targets inflation through money vs full employment through demand.
Changes the owner vs loosens the rules (e.g. Big Bang).
Union victory over Heath vs defeat by Thatcher.

questions.q: What is monetarism and its short-term cost?
questions.r: Priority to inflation via money supply control, spending cuts, high rates; 1980-1981 recession, over 3 million unemployed.

questions.q: Give four privatisations with dates.
questions.r: BT 1984, British Gas 1986, BA and Rolls-Royce 1987, water 1989 (electricity 1990-1991).

questions.q: How did Thatcher fall?
questions.r: Not by election: poll tax anger, Europe divisions, Howe's resignation speech, Heseltine's challenge; she withdrew in Nov 1990, Major succeeded.

chapitres.idee: Major's weakened Conservatives (1990-1997) gave way to Blair's New Labour, which kept the Thatcherite market legacy while adding social investment, devolution and peace in Northern Ireland.
points: Major: council tax, Gulf War (1991), 1992 win, Black Wednesday (16 Sept 1992) = exit from the ERM, credibility lost
Major: Maastricht split (opt-outs: single currency, Social Chapter), sleaze, rail privatisation, Downing Street Declaration (1993)
Blair leader 1994; Clause IV rewritten 1995; Third Way (Giddens): market + education, health, welfare to work
1997-1998: Bank of England independence, minimum wage, Human Rights Act; tarnished by Iraq (2003); Brown 2007
Devolution: powers transferred, Westminster stays sovereign (unitary state); West Lothian question
Good Friday Agreement: consent principle, power-sharing, North-South bodies, decommissioning, prisoner release

dates.fait: Devolution referendums (big Yes Scotland, narrow Yes Wales)
Good Friday Agreement signed; twin referendums 22 May 1998
Scottish Parliament (Holyrood) and Welsh Assembly (now Senedd) elected

distinctions.difference: Westminster remains sovereign vs guaranteed shared sovereignty.
Market + social investment vs nationalisation and unions.

questions.q: What was Black Wednesday and its consequence?
questions.r: 16 Sept 1992: sterling forced out of the ERM; Conservatives lose economic credibility.

questions.q: Define the Third Way.
questions.r: Giddens: beyond state socialism and neoliberalism; accept the market and Thatcher legacy, invest in education, health, welfare to work.

questions.q: What is the West Lothian question?
questions.r: Scottish MPs at Westminster vote on laws that concern only England.

questions.q: Main principles of the Good Friday Agreement?
questions.r: Consent of the majority, power-sharing Assembly and Executive, North-South and East-West bodies, decommissioning, prisoner release.

chapitres.idee: A commentary presents, explains and interprets a document in its historical context: outside knowledge and critical distance, never paraphrase.
points: Identify: nature, author, date, source, audience
Contextualise the political, economic and social situation
Central question on the document's historical interest
Thematic outline in 2-3 parts (not line by line)
Short quotations with line numbers + precise knowledge (dates, laws, actors)
Significance and limits: point of view, intentions, omissions; conclusion answers the question and opens
chapitres.memo: Present, Place, Problem, Plan, Prove, Perspective.

questions.q: What goes into the introduction?
questions.r: Presentation (nature, author, date, source, audience, context), central question, outline.

questions.q: Give a central question for Thatcher's 1980 conference speech.
questions.r: How does this speech assert Thatcherism's break with the post-war consensus?

questions.q: Two phrases to criticise a document?
questions.r: 'However, the author fails to mention...' / 'This view should be qualified...'

parCoeur: 1942 Beveridge Report; five giants: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness
July 1945 Attlee wins; 5 July 1948 NHS (Bevan), free, tax-funded
Butskellism (1954) = Butler + Gaitskell: consensus on Welfare State, mixed economy, Keynesianism
Devaluations 1949 and 1967; stop-go; 'sick man of Europe'
Europe: EFTA 1960, vetoes 1963 and 1967, entry 1 Jan 1973, referendum 1975 (about 67% Yes), Brexit 2016/2020
Crisis: three-day week 1974, IMF 1976, Winter of Discontent 1978-1979, Thatcher May 1979
Privatisations: BT 1984, Gas 1986, BA 1987, water 1989, electricity 1990-1991; Right to Buy 1980
Miners' strike March 1984 - March 1985; Big Bang 27 Oct 1986; Thatcher resigns Nov 1990
Black Wednesday 16 Sept 1992; Maastricht ratified 1993; New Labour 1 May 1997
Clause IV rewritten 1995; Bank of England independent 1997; minimum wage and Human Rights Act 1998
Good Friday Agreement 10 April 1998 (referendums 22 May); devolved bodies elected 1999
Commons: 650 MPs, FPTP; Parliament Acts 1911, 1949 limit the Lords
pieges: Saying the UK has 'no constitution': it is uncodified, not absent.
Crediting the Beveridge Report to Labour: Beveridge was a Liberal under the wartime coalition; Attlee implemented it.
Confusing the Winter of Discontent (1978-1979, Callaghan) with the miners' strike (1984-1985, Thatcher), or the 1974 strike (won) with 1984-1985 (lost).
Saying Thatcher lost an election: she was ousted by her own party in Nov 1990.
Confusing privatisation (owner changes) with deregulation (rules loosened), or devolution with federalism.
Paraphrasing the document instead of explaining it with outside knowledge and a thematic outline.
